title: Compact diagonal images of countably many finite coordinates
statement:
Use [def-weil-size-convention]. Let $S$ be a compact Hausdorff space, let $G$ be a compact Hausdorff topological group, and, for each $n\in\mathbf N$, let $A_n$ be a finite discrete space and $B_n$ a finite group with the discrete topology. Suppose $p_n:S\to A_n$ is continuous and $q_n:G\to B_n$ is a continuous group homomorphism. No surjectivity of the coordinate maps is assumed. Define
$$P(s)=(p_n(s))_n,\qquad Q(g)=(q_n(g))_n,\qquad S_0=P(S)\subseteq\prod_n A_n,\qquad G_0=Q(G)\subseteq\prod_n B_n,$$
with product topologies on the ambient products and subspace topologies [def-kun-subspace-topology] on the images. The corestrictions $p:S\to S_0$ and $q:G\to G_0$ are continuous surjections. The space $S_0$ is compact Hausdorff, has a basis of clopen subsets, and is metrizable. The image $G_0$ is a subgroup with coordinatewise operations, those operations are continuous, and $q$ is a group homomorphism. The space $G_0$ is compact Hausdorff and metrizable, and the open normal subgroups
$$K_F=\{b\in G_0:b_n=1\text{ for every }n\in F\},\qquad F\subseteq\mathbf N\text{ finite},$$
form a neighbourhood basis of its identity. Thus $S_0$ is a metrizable profinite space and $G_0$ a metrizable profinite group. For $s,s'\in S$ one has $p(s)=p(s')$ if and only if $p_n(s)=p_n(s')$ for every $n$; likewise $q(g)=q(g')$ if and only if $q_n(g)=q_n(g')$ for every $n$. Empty $S$ and empty $A_n$ are allowed whenever the given maps exist.

proof.text: For a product of discrete spaces, basic opens prescribe membership in specified subsets at finitely many coordinates. The inverse image under $P$ of such a basic open is a finite intersection of the open sets $p_n^{-1}(U_n)$, hence is open. Thus $P$ is continuous; replacing $p_n$ by $q_n$ proves continuity of $Q$. By [def-kun-subspace-topology], an open of $S_0$ is $S_0\cap V$ for ambient open $V$; its inverse image under $p$ is $P^{-1}(V)$. Therefore $p$ is continuous, and the identical calculation proves continuity of $q$. Each is surjective because its codomain is its image.

source.place: Tag 08ZS, section-limits, opening definition of the product topology; Tag 004E, item-induced-topology. Elementary inverse-image calculation.

proof.text: Apply [lem-weil-pbc-continuous-image-quasi-compact] to $P:S\to\prod_n A_n$ and $Q:G\to\prod_n B_n$. The domains are compact by hypothesis and both maps are continuous by step 1. Hence their images $S_0$ and $G_0$, with exactly the specified induced topologies, are compact. No claim about surjectivity onto either ambient product is needed.

Let $T$ be either image and write $D_n=A_n$ or $B_n$ respectively. For $t\in T$ and finite $F\subseteq\mathbf N$, put $C_F(t)=\{u\in T:u_n=t_n\ (n\in F)\}$. Each cylinder $C_F(t)$ is open and closed: a singleton and its complement are open in each discrete $D_n$, coordinate projections are continuous by the definition of product topology, and finite intersections preserve both properties. Every open neighbourhood of $t$ in $T$ contains such a cylinder, since in an ambient basic open containing $t$ each of its finitely many coordinate conditions can be shrunk to $\{t_n\}$. Thus the cylinders form a clopen basis. Distinct $t,u$ differ in some coordinate $n$, and the disjoint cylinders $C_{\{n\}}(t)$ and $C_{\{n\}}(u)$ separate them. Both images are therefore Hausdorff. Also a connected subset containing distinct $t,u$ would be separated by that cylinder and its complement, so every connected subset has at most one point.

source.place: Tag 08ZS, section-limits, product basis, restricted using the induced topology; Tag 004E, item-Hausdorff. All separation and clopen assertions are proved explicitly from the basis.

proof.text:
Give each $A_n$ and $B_n$ the discrete metric $d(x,y)=0$ when $x=y$ and $1$ otherwise. The triangle inequality follows because if $x
e z$, at least one of $x
e y$ and $y
e z$ holds; balls of radius $1/2$ are singletons, so this metric induces the discrete topology, including on an empty factor. On each compact image, the coordinate projections are continuous by step 3 and separate distinct points because tuples equal in every coordinate are equal. Apply [lem-sfb-compact-countable-separating-metrizable] first with $X=S_0$, $Y_n=A_n$, then with $X=G_0$, $Y_n=B_n$. This proves metrizability for both images, without any completeness or nonemptiness assumption.

source.place: Metric.PiNatEmbed.TopologicalSpace.MetrizableSpace.of_countable_separating, lines 1091-1097; elementary discrete metric supplies its metric target hypotheses.

proof.text: For $g,h\in G$, the homomorphism identities in each coordinate give $Q(1)=(1)_n$, $Q(gh)=Q(g)Q(h)$ and $Q(g^{-1})=Q(g)^{-1}$. Hence $G_0$ contains the identity and is closed under coordinatewise multiplication and inverse, and $q$ is a group homomorphism. These operations are continuous directly on cylinders: the inverse image of $\{b:b_n=a\}$ under multiplication is $\bigcup_{uv=a}(\{b:b_n=u\}\times\{c:c_n=v\})$, open in $G_0\times G_0$; under inversion it is $\{b:b_n=a^{-1}\}$. Inverse images commute with finite intersections and unions, and the coordinate cylinders generate the topology by step 3. Thus both operations are continuous for the given subspace topology, without putting any new topology on $G_0$.

source.place: Tag 0B1Z, definition-topological-group; Tag 08ZS, section-limits. Elementary coordinate computation of inverse images establishes the topological group structure.

proof.text: At the identity, $K_F=C_F(1)$, so each $K_F$ is open by step 3. It is a subgroup because products and inverses of tuples equal to $1$ on $F$ still equal $1$ there. For $b\in G_0$ and $k\in K_F$, one has $(bkb^{-1})_n=b_n1b_n^{-1}=1$ for $n\in F$. Thus conjugation preserves $K_F$; applying this also with $b^{-1}$ gives equality and normality. Every identity neighbourhood contains an open neighbourhood and then some $C_F(1)=K_F$ by step 3. This proves exactly the required neighbourhood basis. The empty finite set gives $K_\varnothing=G_0$. Together with steps 2--4 this proves that $S_0$ is a metrizable profinite space and $G_0$ a metrizable profinite group.

source.place: Tag 08ZS, section-limits, product basis at the identity; Tag 0B1Z, definition-topological-group. Elementary coordinate subgroup and conjugation computations.

proof.text: Equality in an image subtype is equality of its underlying tuple, and tuple equality is equality in every coordinate. Consequently $p(s)=p(s^\prime)$ if and only if $p_n(s)=p_n(s^\prime)$ for every $n$; the same argument gives the assertion for $q$. If $S$ is empty, so is $S_0$, all assertions about its points are vacuous and the compactness and metrizability lemmas above still apply. If some $A_n$ is empty, existence of $p_n$ forces $S$ empty. Finite groups $B_n$ contain their identity, and $Q(1)$ always belongs to $G_0$. No step has assumed a coordinate map surjective. All products and image subsets are formed in the fixed universes of [def-weil-size-convention].
